title: The importance of considering polysubstance use: Lessons from cocaine research

claims.statement: In the samples one review found, a large share of people who use cocaine also used alcohol, and in most samples cannabis, on the same occasions or in the same period, but the share varied widely with the sample and with the definition used. The review combined 16 estimates (11 studies from one PubMed search, January 1990 to June 2017, and 5 of the authors' own analyses of US data sets; 10 from the USA, 3 from Canada, 2 from Brazil and 1 from Denmark; study years 1985 to 2017; samples ranging from household surveys to treatment services, emergency departments, raves and drug courts; all but one by self-report; confidence in the review rated critically low on its study card). Its random-effects averages were 74% (95% CI 50% to 89%) for alcohol and 38% (20% to 60%) for cannabis used at the same time as cocaine or within a couple of hours, and 77% (62% to 87%) for alcohol and 64% (47% to 79%) for cannabis used in the same period (from the past 30 days to a lifetime), with heterogeneity of 97% to 99% in all four; single sources ranged from about a quarter to nearly everyone, and the lowest figures came from the narrowest question: in two St Louis samples of women who had used cocaine in the past 30 days, 23.5% and 36.1% said they had used alcohol to come down from cocaine, while 79.5% and 71.3% had drunk alcohol that month. This matters for research on cocaine: of the 40 most recent human brain-imaging studies of cocaine up to January 2018, none excluded people who drink alcohol or use cannabis (10 excluded alcohol dependence and 10 cannabis dependence), so unless these drugs were accounted for, their findings may mix effects of cocaine with effects of alcohol or cannabis; of 40 recent animal studies of cocaine, 2 also gave alcohol and none gave cannabis, so those animal studies did not model how people combine these drugs (Liu et al., 2018). Tobacco, which the authors think may be combined with other drugs even more often, was not counted; the sources were not appraised, the ranges in the text do not all match the review's table, and how many sources entered each average was shown only in a figure that could not be read. What happens in the body when cocaine and alcohol are taken together is in the answer on mixing cocaine and alcohol. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Liu et al. (2018), random-effects pooled prevalence among people who use cocaine: simultaneous alcohol 74% (95% CI 50–89%), simultaneous cannabis 38% (20–60%), concurrent alcohol 77% (62–87%), concurrent cannabis 64% (47–79%); I² 97–99%; ranges across sources as stated in the text 24–98%, 12–76%, 37–96% and 43–94% (the review's table gives 23.5–87%, 9.3–76.5% and 34.9–96.5% for the first three); number of sources in each estimate not readable (figure not viewable). St Louis women's samples (n = 463 and 122): alcohol used to come down from cocaine 23.5% and 36.1%, cannabis 9.3% and 12.3%, any past-30-day alcohol 79.5% and 71.3%. Research count: of 40 human cocaine imaging studies, none excluded people who drink or use cannabis, 10 excluded alcohol dependence and 10 cannabis dependence; of 40 animal cocaine studies, 2 gave alcohol and none cannabis; co-use present or modelled in 75% vs 5% (alcohol) and 72.5% vs 0% (cannabis) of human vs animal studies (Fisher's exact p < 0.0001), percentages that measure different things in the two kinds of study.
